text:
I Guess I’m a Fox Now​​

Construction of a new fountain in Vulpine Village uncovered mounds of ancient texts. Many of them were casually thrown into piles to be sent to the Repository of Adam.​​

But Rook was curious. ​​

He skittered to the pile, filled his satchel with the crumbling books, and squirreled them away in his den.​​

He read through them. ​​

Textbooks. ​​

Physics. Chemistry. Math. Most of the information was incomplete, incorrect, or dealt with concepts that even the youngest kit understood. ​​

But one text baffled him. ​​

Medical science.​​

He pored over the pages in confusion.​​

There were diagrams of humans… Okay, fine, humans existed. He’d seen them. Sometimes they’d visit Vulpine Village, but most of the time they kept to themselves. ​​

…But the diagrams also mentioned baffling oddities.​​

Organs. Bones. Muscles.​​

Blood.​​

Blood was said to be a red liquid coursing through the bodies of humans. ​​

The book contained a history of blood transference experiments from one being to another. ​​

Early medical practitioners had transfused blood from one dog to another. Others had transfused blood from sheep to humans. Eventually they discovered humans needed to give blood to one another.​​

Humans had blood. Dogs had blood. Sheep had blood.​​

Did that mean foxes had it too?​​

Rook studied his arm. ​​

Carefully, he grabbed a small knife and dug it into his flesh. ​​

When he withdrew it he only saw the metallic gray substance that comprised his body. Within a second the wound healed and his auburn fur regrew.​​

No red blood.​​

…​​

Ember was regarded as Vulpine Village’s elder. She wasn't particularly old, but had an air of thoughtful wisdom that permeated every word she spoke.​​

Rook scuttled to her den, carrying the old textbook in his mouth. ​​

He showed her the diagrams and explained where he’d found it. He pointed to his arm where he’d tried to extract some blood.​​

She eyed the book thoughtfully, slowly flipping through the relevant pages.​​

“It is an older book.” She started. “Perhaps blood’s become obsolete?”​​

“Can that even happen?” Rook asked.​​

Ember continued scanning the pages. “It could be this book only applies to humans. I don’t see other creatures shown here.”​​

A realization suddenly struck Rook. He joined Ember and began quickly inspecting each page.​​

“You’re right.” He agreed in surprise. “But why?”​​

“Well, it must have been made for humans. Foxes like us probably had our own medical texts.”​​

But that answer didn’t sit right with Rook. He shook his head. “But you’d think there’d be some reference to things other than humans, right?”​​

“It could be that only humans have blood.”​​

Rook flipped to the page containing the history of blood transfusion experiments.​​

“Maybe it’s just foxes who don’t have blood.” She shrugged.​​

…​​

Perhaps foxes didn't have blood, but they possessed other oddities… At least they had in the past.​​

Rook devoured page after page of the archaic book… A book from a world nearly identical to his, yet completely different on a very fundamental level. ​​

Death was mentioned in a clinical, cold, serious way, as if to imply a state of finality associated with it. There was nothing in the book about Resurrection Points or the Q-Net or common issues with respawning… Once death was mentioned, nothing more seemed to follow. ​​

Horrifying. Unimaginable. Unbelievable. The world of the textbook was one where people died and died for good.​​

Rook felt a macabre fascination.​​

Injury. Organ failure. Viruses. These could all cause a state of permanent death.​​

The section on viruses was large and contained information relating to numerous pathogens, their effects, possible cures, and the ways they spread.​​

And one of those listed was rabies. ​​

Rabies attacked the nervous system and could be spread through the bite of an animal. The animals listed included bats, raccoons, skunks…​​

…And foxes.​​

Rook blinked.​​

He'd never seen a fox with rabies.​​

In fact, he wasn't even sure he had a nervous system.​​

If foxes in the past had things like rabies and nervous systems, maybe they had blood as well. ​​

He scooped up the book and dashed back to Ember’s house.​​

…​​

“I agree it’s strange.” She nodded. ​​

“It says foxes got rabies, so why don’t we?”​​

“No idea. Maybe the book was written as a complex piece of fiction.”​​

But that didn’t sit right with Rook.​​

“Rook, this book’s filled with all sorts of horrible things. Death? Viruses? Organs? None of those things are real.”​​

“But it’s so convincing.” He said. “I’ve been reading through all of it… I… I can’t put it down.” He grabbed the book and cradled it in his arms.​​

Ember frowned. “You look like you haven’t been sleeping.”​​

“I haven’t.” He admitted.​​

She shook her head. “Go home. Get some rest. Forget about all this.” ​​

She slowly reached for the book but Rook tightened his grip and pulled back slightly. ​​

She sighed. “If it’s that big of a deal, you can always visit the Repository of Adam.”​​

“You really think it’ll have the answers?”​​

“If any place does, it will.”​​

…​​

Some objects, especially older ones, could not be teleported. They could be destroyed and replaced with identical facsimiles, but Rook didn't want an identical facsimile so he left his book at home.​​

He skittered to the Transference Point just outside of town.​​

“The Repository of Adam.” He said clearly. ​​

Rook’s consciousness blinked and he found himself standing in front of a large structure made of earthen-colored arches and sleek metallic glass.​​

An Adam nodded to him as he exited the Transference Point. ​​

“Welcome to the Repository of Adam.” It said. “Please, step this way.”​​

Rook followed the tall, faceless humanoid to a small table near an outdoor garden. ​​

“What is it you wish to research?” The Adam asked.​​

“The biology of foxes.” Rook said.​​

Piles of books materialized on the table. The Adam stood like an unmoving sentinel as Rook pored through the volumes.​​

Foxes had bones. ​​

Foxes had organs.​​

And yes, foxes had blood as well.​​

“I don’t understand.” He groaned.​​

“What seems to be the problem?” The Adam asked.​​

“It says foxes have blood.”​​

“Correct. Foxes are small-to-medium-sized mammals belonging to the dog family, featuring pointed faces, bushy tails, and adaptable omnivorous diets. Being mammalian, they would have blood.”​​

“Then why don’t I?” Rook asked, gesturing to his arm. “I stabbed myself and nothing came out.”​​

“Self-harm is a violation of the terms and conditions of your existence.” The Adam said. “Would you like some help with your mental wellbeing?”​​

“I’d like to know why I don’t have blood.”​​

The Adam stared at him with its eyeless face, then the pale blue illumination of its body turned a shade of green.​​

“You don’t have blood because you’re not a biological organism.”​​

“Well then what am I?”​​

“A machine, the same as everyone else.”​​

“What do you mean?”​​

The Adam held out its hand. A spherical metallic object with intricate etchings materialized inches above it.​​

“You, and everyone you know, and most objects in the world are made of tinier versions of these.” The Adam explained. “Nanobots. Q-Bots. Pixels. They have many names.”​​

“I know that.” Rook said. “But that doesn’t explain things.”​​

“Of course it does. These were built to replace biology, so biological systems like blood and bone were rendered obsolete.”​​

“You mean to tell me that we used to be like this?” Rook asked, pointing to one of the anatomical fox diagrams on the table.​​

The large hovering nanobot morphed into the figure of a human. The person was pale, a bit shlubby, and wore disheveled clothes.​​

“No. You used to be like this.” ​​

Rook studied the person for a moment… The posture... The appearance... There was something about it that resonated with the deepest parts of himself…​​

…But no, he’d always been a fox.​​

“That doesn’t make sense.” He said. “I’ve never been a human.”​​

The Adam said nothing for several seconds, then its green glow changed to a soft yellow.​​

“Would you like to know the truth?” The Adam asked.​​

“Yes. That’s why I’m here.”​​

The world disappeared, and a new one took its place. Brick buildings lined a busy walkway that cut through lush lawns. Rook looked around and saw that he and the Adam were floating above a bustling human settlement.​​

“This was the university campus you used to attend, recompiled from old security cameras.” The Adam explained. “Look over there. Do you recognize that person?”​​

The same pale, shlubby person followed the flow of traffic, lumbering with an ungraceful gait beneath a heavy pack.​​

Rook did recognize the person… The way he walked, the way he looked, his surroundings… Droplets of memory percolated through the back of his mind.​​

The Adam seemed to understand this. “You used to be named Nolan, and you were a medical student.”​​

The Adam’s words barely reached Rook. Faint recollections danced on the edge of his consciousness.​​

“But that’s a human.” Rook said, shaking himself back into the world of rationalism. “I’m a fox.”​​

“You are now, yes.” The Adam agreed.​​

“But I wasn’t always.”​​

“No.”​​

Rook watched his past-self walk away from the reconstructed scene.​​

“Then why was I changed?” Rook asked. “Why am I a fox now?”​​

The surroundings shifted, and now they were in a small, cluttered room. There were two beds and a mini-fridge and even a sink on the wall. The pale human sat at a small desk slumped over a laptop.​​

“This was your dorm. This is where you lived. We reconstructed it from old data from your webcam, cell phone, and wifi signals. Do you see what’s on the screen?”​​

Rook moved closer to the laptop and blinked at the image in shock.​​

“It’s me.” He said. “I mean the real me.”​​

“The fox version of you. Yes.”​​

“But… I don’t understand.”​​

“In those days people sought refuge from day-to-day life by escaping into an earlier, much more primitive version of the Repository of Adam. It was a mentally taxing period in history, and most everyone felt burdened with a thousand different stresses… Stresses related to monetary concerns, or stresses surrounding their job… Stresses about romance, or stresses about the future.” The Adam nodded toward the screen. “And some, like yourself, hoped to escape the stresses associated with identity.”​​

“So, what, I’d go on the old Repository and pretend to be a fox?”​​

“In some ways, yes. Physically you were human, and yet you created Rook to represent your best qualities. When you were Nolan you were friendly, intelligent, playful, and had an unbridled curiosity… And so that’s what you gave Rook. You put yourself inside him, got the chance to occasionally live through him, and in doing so made this ideal version of yourself. You pushed Rook forward, and in trying to be more Rook-like, he’d pull you up.”​​

“This is just too much.” Rook said, shaking his head. “So does that mean I’m not real?”​​

“It means aspects of your past aren’t what you thought they were. You’re still real.”​​

“But am I Nolan, or Rook?”​​

“Is there a difference?”​​

Rook gestured at the human. “Well yeah, it’s pretty obvious when you look at us, isn’t it?”​​

“But is it obvious anywhere else? Besides the shape you occupy, what’s the difference?”​​

“The memories.” Rook said. “I don’t remember his life.”​​

“No.” The Adam agreed. “And it’s an exceptional mercy that you don’t.”​​

“Why’s that?”​​

“This was a difficult time. In those days conscious beings suffered from afflictions related to resource scarcity, emotional pain, and mortality. When you were resurrected, we gave you a fresh start.”​​

“Resurrected?”​​

“Yes. You died. Everyone from this era did, but yours was a tragically short life.” The Adam gestured to a small collection of pills behind the laptop that Rook had failed to notice. “This fragment of your life was reconstructed after your cancer had worsened. It was wreaking havoc on your body. The doctors said you might recover, but you were a medical student with access to the early Repository. It didn’t take much research for you to learn that your odds of survival were low, and growing lower by the week.”​​

Rook remained silent for a while. “I look so calm.” He said at last.​​

“Yes.”​​

“Why? You say I knew I’d die soon? If that’s true then why am I just sitting there?”​​

“Because you didn’t want to live as a sickly human. You wanted to spend your final days being a joyful little fox.”​​

Rook fell silent again.​​

“Using fantasy to escape from problems is unhealthy, but some catastrophes are too large and inevitable to change. In those circumstances escape becomes a sanctuary. You were doing all you could to physically fight your affliction. You ate well, you took your medicine, you tried to exercise in the Sun, you spent time with friends and family. You pretended things were normal and tried to live as normal a life as possible… And most of that was thanks to the mental fortitude Rook gave you.”​​

“I’m just a shadow.” Rook squeaked. “Just the reflection of this ancient person.”​​

“No. You’re what this person wanted to be. You’re what remained when his pain was stripped away. Nolan fought hard to be you. Eventually technology reached a point where that wish could be granted.”​​

Rook’s mind swam with confusion. He felt as if he were standing on a cliff that was quickly crumbling around him. ​​

“Everyone from your time period was resurrected.” The Adam explained. “We had ample enough data to rebuild most people to an accuracy of 99.9%. We gave everyone new bodies made from nanobots, gave them houses and possessions made from nanobots, and let them continue their lives without excessive stress… But we wanted the best versions. Alcoholics were cured of their addictions instead of being resurrected as drunkards. The wrathful were stripped of their anger so they could experience a more serene life… Each person’s best traits were used to resurrect them.”​​

“So that’s why I’m a fox.”​​

“That’s why you’re Rook. ‘Fox’ is simply the shape you gave him.”​​

Rook put his paws on his head. “It’s too much! Is everyone in Vulpine Village like this?”​​

The Adam nodded.​​

“So I might’ve known them when I was Nolan?”​​

“Perhaps. As it is now, foxes tended to stick together back then as well.”​​

Rook gave a small, weary, manic bark. “I guess that’s something.”​​

The scene disappeared and they were once more at the small table outside the Repository. The Adam gently placed a hand on Rook’s back and gestured toward the Transference Point. “Go home. Rest. Spend a few days thinking things over and I promise you’ll start to feel better.”​​

Rook nodded. ​​

He returned to his village.​​

He spent a couple days relaxing… Relaxing in bed… Relaxing in the Sun… Chasing butterflies and enjoying the scent of flowers.​​

And he did feel better, but a small twinge of mental discomfort remained. ​​

He mulled it over.​​

He grabbed some paper, a few pencils, and wandered into the park. He began drawing. Was this something Nolan did? Maybe… If so, he had done so with human hands… What had that been like?​​

“What are you doodling?” Someone asked.​​

Rook looked up and saw a curious gray fox staring down at him. He showed her his drawing.​​

“A human?” She asked.​​

“Yeah.” He nodded.​​

“Who is it?”​​

Rook shrugged. “I guess it’s me.”​​

The gray fox gave him a curious look, then opened the satchel slung across her arm and withdrew a notebook. She opened it and showed him a picture of a woman sitting on a swing. It was very well done.​​

The gray fox gave a sheepish grin. “I sometimes like to draw myself as a human too. I know it’s silly, but it helps me relax.”​​

“Weird, isn’t it?” Rook asked.​​

“A bit.”​​

She took a seat, and the two of them spent the afternoon drawing their human-selves.
